sentiment.title: Market pulse
sentiment.pulse_help: The white pin is today; the grey one is a month ago. Every input is scored against its own last 252 sessions, so this reads "for this year" — never in absolute terms.
sentiment.pulse_missing: Not included right now: {names}. The score is quoted on {live} of {total} inputs; below {floor} the pin parks mid-scale under an "n/a".
sentiment.indices_pinned: Ordered by the geography your portfolio actually holds.
sentiment.risk_help: The percentile pair is the whole reading: p12 (37) is the 12th percentile of its own year today, the 37th a month ago. A VIX that is calm and newly calm says whether the regime is settling or turning; a percentile is never an absolute verdict.
sentiment.rates_help: The change is in basis points, not percent: a "+7.4%" on a 4.79% yield reads like a price move and is not one. The two curve rows and the two policy rates print uncoloured — a rise is not the bad direction there, the warning is inversion.
sentiment.us10y_help: Nominal 10-year Treasury yield — the discount rate every long-duration asset is priced off.
sentiment.us10y_real_help: 10-year TIPS yield: the nominal yield stripped of expected inflation. Unprofitable growth moves against this one, not the nominal.
sentiment.curve_2s10s_help: 10-year minus 2-year. Negative is an inverted curve — historically a recession lead, with long and unreliable timing.
sentiment.curve_3m10y_help: 10-year minus 3-month. The variant with the better recession record, and the one that reacts first to policy.
sentiment.hy_spread_help: Option-adjusted spread of US junk bonds over Treasuries. The cleanest single stress gauge there is: it widens before equity volatility arrives.
sentiment.ig_spread_help: Investment-grade option-adjusted spread. Widening here, not just in junk, is stress reaching solid borrowers.
sentiment.breakeven5y_help: Inflation the bond market is pricing for the next five years — expectations, not a print.
sentiment.policy_fed_help: Upper bound of the Fed's target range.
sentiment.policy_ecb_help: ECB deposit facility rate — the euro's policy rate in practice.
sentiment.inflation_help: Annual rate. Euro-area HICP from Eurostat, US CPI from FRED — they do not publish on the same calendar, so each row carries its own reference month.
sentiment.rotation_help: The reading here is a comparison down a column ("who led?"), not a row that reads on its own. Your weight and Tilt appear only with a book; a sector you do not hold counts as zero, because not holding it is an active position and hiding it would hide your biggest underweights.
sentiment.rotation_capture: Your sector mix caught {value} of this month's rotation, weighted by your own positions.
sentiment.factors_help: Each pair rises when the first side leads. Read as a tilt, not a switch.
sentiment.cross_help: The cross-asset read behind the equity move. The dollar reaches you twice: here as a price, and in your book as part of its market value.
sentiment.book_signed_out: Sign in and import your transactions to read this regime against your own positions.
sentiment.book_empty: No open positions yet — import your transactions and this card reads the regime against your own book.
sentiment.book_help: Betas are measured on your current weights over the last 12 months: a reading of what you hold now, not of how it has performed.
sentiment.beta_equity_help: How much your basket moves for each 1% of the index. Above 1 amplifies both directions.
sentiment.beta_duration_help: Sensitivity to long Treasuries (TLT), the rates proxy. Positive means your book gains when yields fall — the long-duration growth profile.
sentiment.beta_credit_help: Sensitivity to high-yield bonds (HYG). High means your names are priced off risk appetite and funding conditions.
sentiment.beta_em_help: Sensitivity to emerging markets (EEM) — global risk appetite, not just the US market.
sentiment.usd_share_help: Share of your market value priced in dollars, and what the dollar's move did to it over the last month. Holding US names in a EUR book is an unhedged short-EUR position whether you wanted one or not.
sentiment.fx_note: Currency moved your value by {value} over the last month, before the assets did anything.
sentiment.note_leading: Leading right now among your largest sectors: {names}.
sentiment.note_lagging: Lagging right now among your largest sectors: {names}.
sentiment.prices_unavailable: The provider is throttling this server. Try again in a moment: every block fails on its own, and whatever does not need prices is still loaded.
sentiment.macro_unavailable: The source is not answering this server. Try again in a moment; the rest of the screen does not depend on it.
sentiment.sources: Prices via Yahoo Finance · rates and credit via FRED · inflation via Eurostat and FRED · loaded {stamp}. Information only, not investment advice.
sentiment.trend_help: Trend compares the level to its own {n}-session average, and that average's short arm to its long one — so an established trend and one that is turning read differently. The line is the last 90 sessions.
sentiment.breadth_sectors_note: trading above their {n}-session average · an index at a high with a third of its sectors below trend is a narrowing market
sentiment.stock_bond_corr_note: positive means both legs fall together and the diversification you think you have is not there
sentiment.nfci_note: Chicago Fed financial conditions index at {value}, {change} over three months. Below zero is looser than average — the funding backdrop behind every spread above.
sentiment.inflation_momentum_help: "vs 6m" is the annual rate now minus the annual rate six months ago, in percentage points: the level says where prices are, this says which way the trend has turned. Not a three-month annualised rate — Eurostat publishes HICP unadjusted for seasonality, and annualising raw months would compound January sales into what looks like a trend.
sentiment.book_bond_corr: Your basket's correlation with long bonds is {value} (was {prior} three months ago) — the higher it is, the more your real risk is rates rather than equities.
sentiment.pulse_stamp: as_of {date} · Yahoo Finance closes + FRED · {live} of {total} inputs live
sentiment.pulse_complete: All {total} inputs are live today: the score is not leaning on a shorter average than it looks.
sentiment.comp_breadth_sub: RSP/SPY 20d · is the average stock keeping up?
sentiment.comp_term_sub: VIX3M/VIX · below 1, hedging now costs more than hedging later
sentiment.comp_credit_sub: HY spread (FRED) · widens before equity vol arrives
sentiment.comp_global_risk_sub: EEM/SPY 20d · the only input that is not a US read
sentiment.snapshot_hint: a level with no history is no reading
sentiment.quad_meaning_bear_steepening: The long end is selling faster than the short: growth or supply, not policy.
sentiment.quad_meaning_bear_flattening: Yields up, curve compressing: inflation, or a central bank running late.
sentiment.quad_meaning_bull_steepening: Yields down with the short end falling faster: cuts are being priced.
sentiment.quad_meaning_bull_flattening: Yields down with the long end falling faster: a growth scare and a bid for duration.
sentiment.side_lede: The market is in {regime} and your basket {stance}: beta {beta} to equities, and {usd} of its value is priced in dollars.
sentiment.side_help: The pill is not a price change: it is the three-month drift of the level itself. A beta that was 0.94 and is 1.18 today means the regime moved under you without you buying anything.
sentiment.side_more: See all five betas and this month's notes ↓
sentiment.book_src: your ledger × Yahoo prices · 1 h cache
sentiment.book_signed_out_note: The composite, the indices and the gauges are still there: they need no account. What is missing here are your basket's betas and your dollar exposure.
sentiment.book_empty_note: There is no honest version of this block for an empty book: no invented betas, no 0% dollar exposure.
sentiment.detail_hint: one shape for every row: level · change over four horizons · 90 sessions · trend state
sentiment.src_fred: {n} series · FRED · publishes a day late, 6 h cache
sentiment.src_inflation: {n} areas · Eurostat HICP + US CPI via FRED · monthly, 24 h cache
sentiment.src_rotation: excess return over the S&P 500 · Yahoo Finance
sentiment.src_factors: {n} pairs · each pair rises when the first side leads
sentiment.src_derived: derived from the prices and from FRED
sentiment.sector_not_held: you hold none: an active underweight
sentiment.tip_index_gspc: The 500 largest US listed companies, weighted by market value. The world's default equity benchmark: most funds, most betas and most headlines saying “the market” mean this.
sentiment.tip_index_ixic: Every common stock listed on Nasdaq, around 3,000 of them, cap-weighted and heavy in technology. It leads the S&P on the way up and on the way down.
sentiment.tip_index_dji: Thirty large US companies weighted by share price rather than size — an accident of 1896 that lets one high-priced stock move it more than a far bigger company. Read it as history, not as a measure.
sentiment.tip_index_rut: The 2,000 smallest names of the Russell 3000: US domestic small caps. They run on floating-rate bank debt, so this is the index that feels a rate rise first.
sentiment.tip_index_stoxx50e: Fifty blue chips of the euro area. Large, exporting and cyclical — the euro's S&P, only far more concentrated.
sentiment.tip_index_gdaxi: Germany's 40 largest listed companies: cars, chemicals and industrial machinery. A bet on global manufacturing and on Chinese demand.
sentiment.tip_index_ibex: Spain's 35 largest listed companies. Banks, utilities and Latin-American exposure dominate it, so it reads rates and the Mexican and Brazilian cycle far more than technology.
sentiment.tip_index_fchi: France's 40 largest listed companies — luxury, energy and banks, with most of the revenue earned outside France.
sentiment.tip_index_ftse: The 100 largest companies on the London exchange: oil, miners and banks, most of them earning in dollars. When sterling falls this usually rises.
sentiment.tip_index_n225: 225 Japanese names, price-weighted like the Dow. A weak yen lifts it, because the earnings behind it are mostly exports.
sentiment.tip_index_hsi: Hong Kong's benchmark, and the accessible proxy for Chinese equity risk. Policy in Beijing moves it more than earnings do.
sentiment.tip_index_acwi: iShares MSCI ACWI — developed and emerging markets in one fund. The closest thing here to “global equities”, and roughly two thirds of it is the US.
sentiment.tip_index_eem: iShares MSCI Emerging Markets: China, Taiwan, Korea, India and Brazil. It trades on the dollar and on global risk appetite as much as on its own earnings.
sentiment.tip_gauge_vix: Annualised volatility the options market is pricing for the S&P 500 over the next 30 days, in percent. Under 15 is calm, over 30 is a market repricing risk. A thermometer of fear, never a forecast of direction.
sentiment.tip_gauge_vxn: The same 30-day implied volatility, on the Nasdaq 100. It normally sits above the VIX, and the gap is what the options market charges for technology's extra beta.
sentiment.tip_gauge_vvix: The volatility of the VIX itself — what options on the VIX cost. It rises when traders start hedging the hedge, which is often before the VIX moves at all.
sentiment.tip_gauge_move: The bond market's VIX: implied volatility on US Treasury options. Rate shocks reach equities through here, so this usually turns first.
sentiment.tip_gauge_ovx: Implied volatility on crude oil. It spikes on supply news — OPEC, war, sanctions — before the oil price itself settles on a direction.
sentiment.tip_gauge_gvz: Implied volatility on gold. A high reading usually means gold is being traded as a macro hedge rather than as a metal.
sentiment.tip_gauge_skew: What far out-of-the-money S&P puts cost relative to at-the-money ones — the price of crash protection. Above 145 someone is paying up for tail risk while the VIX can still look calm.
sentiment.tip_rate_us10y: Read it against the real yield below it: the same rise is inflation expectations if the real yield stays put, and genuinely tighter money if it moves too. Long-duration growth reprices on the second case.
sentiment.tip_rate_us10y_real: The rate that competes with your equities once inflation is stripped out. When it rises, a company whose profits arrive years from now is worth less today with nothing having changed in its business.
sentiment.tip_rate_curve_2s10s: Normal is positive — money costs more for longer. Negative is the market saying policy is tight enough to break something, and historically it is the recovery back through zero, not the inversion itself, that lands near the recession.
sentiment.tip_rate_curve_3m10y: The 3-month leg is where policy actually sits, so this slope moves the day expectations for the Fed move. When it disagrees with 2s10s, the disagreement is about the timing of cuts.
sentiment.tip_rate_hy_spread: The one to watch if you only watch one. Equities fall on bad news; this widens on bad funding, which is what turns a fall into a regime. Under 350bp is complacency, over 500bp is stress.
sentiment.tip_rate_ig_spread: It should barely move. When it does, the trouble has left the weakest borrowers and reached the ones banks and pension funds hold — the point where credit stops being someone else's problem.
sentiment.tip_rate_breakeven5y: The bond market's own inflation forecast, priced daily and revised instantly, so it reads expectations better than any published print can. Central banks watch it to judge whether expectations are still anchored.
sentiment.tip_rate_policy_fed: The rate every other dollar rate is built on. It steps in 25bp moves at eight meetings a year, so a flat line here is not an absence of news — it is the committee holding.
sentiment.tip_rate_policy_ecb: What the ECB pays banks to park cash overnight. Your euro deposit account, your money-market fund and a variable mortgage all follow it, with a lag.
sentiment.tip_area_EA: Harmonised euro-area inflation — the number the ECB targets at 2%, and therefore the one that decides what your euro deposits pay.
sentiment.tip_area_ES: Spain's HICP, on the same basket as the rest of the euro area so the rows are comparable. Running above the euro-area rate means losing price competitiveness inside a currency Spain cannot devalue.
sentiment.tip_area_DE: Germany's HICP: the largest single weight in the euro-area figure, and politically the constraint on how long the ECB can stay loose.
sentiment.tip_area_FR: France's HICP. Regulated energy tariffs damp it, so it turns later than the rest of the bloc in both directions.
sentiment.tip_area_IT: Italy's HICP. A heavy energy importer, so it swings with gas prices more than its neighbours do.
sentiment.tip_area_NL: The Netherlands' HICP. Small, open and quick to pass energy and rent through, so it often leads the euro-area turn.
sentiment.tip_area_PT: Portugal's HICP, measured on the euro area's common basket.
sentiment.tip_area_US: US CPI from FRED, not HICP: a different basket, with owners' equivalent rent as its largest single weight. Not directly comparable to the European rows.
sentiment.tip_sector_technology: Semiconductors, software and hardware (XLK). Long-duration earnings: it leads when rates fall and it is the first thing sold when they rise.
sentiment.tip_sector_financial_services: Banks, insurers and exchanges (XLF). They earn the spread between what they pay for deposits and what they charge for loans, so a steeper curve helps and credit losses hurt.
sentiment.tip_sector_energy: Oil and gas producers, refiners and services (XLE). It tracks the crude price, and it is the one sector that usually rises when an inflation shock arrives.
sentiment.tip_sector_healthcare: Pharma, insurers and device makers (XLV). Demand barely moves with the cycle, so it holds up in a downturn and lags badly in a recovery.
sentiment.tip_sector_consumer_cyclical: What people buy when they feel rich: cars, travel, retail, restaurants (XLY). The purest read on household confidence there is.
sentiment.tip_sector_consumer_defensive: Food, drink, household goods and supermarkets (XLP). Bought in every cycle, so this one leading is usually a defensive market rather than good news.
sentiment.tip_sector_industrials: Machinery, aerospace, rail and freight (XLI). Orders here turn before GDP does.
sentiment.tip_sector_utilities: Regulated electricity, gas and water (XLU). A bond in equity clothing — it trades on the 10-year yield more than on the economy.
sentiment.tip_sector_basic_materials: Miners, chemicals and packaging (XLB). Early-cycle, and tied to Chinese construction more than to anything domestic.
sentiment.tip_sector_real_estate: Listed REITs (XLRE). Rent is the income and debt is the cost, so it is the sector rates hit from both sides at once.
sentiment.tip_sector_communication_servi: Telecoms alongside the ad-funded platforms and studios (XLC). Two businesses in one bucket — a regulated utility and Alphabet/Meta, whose weight decides the sector's move.
sentiment.tip_pair_growth_value: IVW over IVE: the S&P's growth half against its value half. It rises when the market is willing to pay up for earnings that have not arrived yet, which is what falling rates allow.
sentiment.tip_pair_small_large: IWM over SPY: the Russell 2000 against the S&P 500. Small caps carry floating-rate debt and domestic revenue, so this rising is a bet on the home economy and on cuts.
sentiment.tip_pair_equal_cap: RSP over SPY: the same 500 companies equally weighted against cap-weighted. Falling means the index is being carried by its largest handful — the number to check before calling a rally broad.
sentiment.tip_pair_us_world: SPY over ACWX: the US against the rest of the world. It has risen for over a decade, and the dollar plus technology's weight explains most of that.
sentiment.tip_pair_cyclical_defensive: XLY over XLP: what people buy when confident against what they buy regardless. One of the cleanest internal reads on whether the market believes in the cycle.
sentiment.tip_pair_tech_market: XLK over SPY: technology against the index it already dominates. It measures concentration — when this rises, so does your dependence on a handful of names.
sentiment.tip_asset_dx_y_nyb: The dollar against a basket of six currencies, euro-heavy. It sets global financial conditions: a strong dollar drains emerging markets and shrinks what US multinationals earn abroad.
sentiment.tip_asset_eurusd_x: Dollars per euro. Rising means a stronger euro — and a smaller euro value for everything you hold priced in dollars.
sentiment.tip_asset_gc_f: Gold futures, dollars per troy ounce. It pays no coupon, so it competes against real yields; central-bank buying has been the other half of the story.
sentiment.tip_asset_si_f: Silver futures, dollars per ounce. Half precious metal, half industrial input for solar and electronics, which is why it travels further than gold in both directions.
sentiment.tip_asset_cl_f: West Texas Intermediate crude futures, the US oil benchmark, in dollars per barrel. An input cost for most of the economy and the revenue line for the energy sector.
sentiment.tip_asset_hg_f: Copper futures, dollars per pound. It goes into everything that gets built or wired, so its price is a live vote on global construction — China's above all.
sentiment.tip_asset_btc_usd: Bitcoin in dollars, traded around the clock. It has behaved as the market's highest-beta risk asset far more than as digital gold.
sentiment.tip_asset_eth_usd: Ether in dollars. It follows bitcoin's direction with more amplitude, plus its own supply and staking mechanics.
